newsitem.title: MACAU: Macau poll shows big business' power to mobilise.
newsitem.headline: Macau poll shows big business' power to mobilise.

text.p: The success of big business in Macau's election revealed that local tycoons could mobilise the population better than pro-China groups, and Beijing could not control voting in the enclave, analysts said on Tuesday.

Three "big-business" groups representing casino, property and entertainment interests dominated the result of Sunday's legislative poll, the last in the Portuguese-ruled enclave before Lisbon hands it back to China in 1999.
Many of those who voted for Macau's three "big-business" groups are either members of their workforce, or their family members and business associates, local sources said.

"In Macau, workers are loyal to their bosses, especially in the entertainment, gambling and property sectors, and that's why these three groups have won half of the eight directly elected seats at stake," a Macau government election official said.
Some local community leaders voiced concern that reputed triad gangster kingpins might try to enter the Macau Legislative Assembly to gain social respectability before the 1999 handover.
Macau was rife with rumours on Sunday that some of the 12 groups contesting the election had paid voters 1,000 to 3,000 patacas (US$125-375) to vote for a particular group.
Re-elected pro-democracy legislator Ng Kuo Cheong, dubbed as Macau's perennial political underdog by local analysts, complained to media about alleged vote-buying by some groups.
Some voters were brought to polling stations on buses after receiving free meals from campaigners, although the numbers were unclear, local sources said.
But election commission chief Rodrigo Leal de Carvalho said the allegations of electoral fraud "did not compromise the seriousness of the election process".
Other government officials said there had been "no specific cases (of vote-buying) to prompt legal action".
"The outcome of the direct elections is proof that China is unable to control the balloting in Macau," a political analyst in the territory said.
Pro-China groups in the past have often been the strongest force in the contest for legislative seats in this territory of 424,000 people on the south China coast.
An editorial in the influential Portuguese-language daily Futuro de Macau described the strong "entrepreneurial wave" highlighted by the poll as a "most perverse reversion".

"Rough money won Macau's last legislative elections under Portuguese rule," a senior civil servant of the Macau administration said. "Now the legislature at least is a better mirror of Macau's economic structure," he added, referring to the casino industry's dominance in the economy.
But Macau governor General Vasco Rocha Vieira, in a comment to the media on the election, said it had "consolidated and strengthened" the territory's political system.
About one-third of Macau's workforce work in the casino tourism sector, the local economy's biggest revenue earner.
In terms of votes, the three "big business" electoral groups won one third of the votes and half of the seats at stake, while the pro-China camp lost one of its previous four seats.
It was the first time in two decades of direct legislative elections in Macau that "big-business" groups took part.

Only eight seats in the 23-seat Legislative Assembly are directly elected. Another eight are indirectly elected on nominations from functional constituencies representing business, labour, and community associations.
The other seven deputies are appointed by the colonial governor after the elections.
